Breaking the Marmont Cipher1809

A Napoleonic war briefing, unread for 217 years

abstract

A letter to General Marmont has sat on the standard list of unsolved historical ciphers, known only from a single reproduction in a 1969 French army journal that carries the wrong date.[1] This post gives a full working reading, produced end-to-end from that single scanned plate, redates the letter to March 1809, and places it in the two weeks before Austria invaded Bavaria. The full solution package, with a script that regenerates the reading, is available for download.

Two weeks before the war

In February 1809, Vienna decided on war.[23] Napoleon had deposed the Spanish Bourbons the previous spring and taken their kingdom for his brother, and Vienna concluded that the Habsburgs were next unless it struck while his best troops were tied down in Spain.[24][23] On 8 February the Austrian Empire resolved to fight Napoleon, with the war party pointing at the French disaster at Bailén in Spain, where an entire French corps had surrendered the previous July.[26][25] Archduke Charles was the Austrian Emperor's younger brother and the best general the Habsburgs had.[19] He had spent three years rebuilding the army: 340,000 regulars, plus a new Landwehr militia on paper at 240,000.[26][27] Everyone could see what was coming.

Napoleon had a specific problem, and its name was Marmont.

Marmont, a personal friend of the Emperor, had been entrusted with what were called the "finest" troops in the theater (about 13,000 men by Napoleon's own count), and they were parked in Dalmatia on the far side of the Adriatic.[29][11] Austrian territory sat between them and every other French army. If war came, Marmont would be the most isolated general in the Empire.

So on 16 March 1809, Napoleon wrote from Paris to his stepson Eugène, the Viceroy of Italy, and told him to send Marmont a letter.[18] It was to lay out where every French and allied army stood. It was to go "dans une lettre chiffrée et par un officier intelligent": in cipher, carried by an intelligent officer.[10]

That letter, or one written to exactly that order, survives. Its first line is in plain French:[3]

Vous avez dû recevoir, Monsieur le Général Marmont, mes lettres des 8, 14 et 20 courant.

then 24 rows of cipher

After that come twenty-four rows of two-digit numbers, stray letters, and invented symbols.

The key didn't survive, and for 217 years nobody alive could read it.

Why this one

I've never broken a cipher. A week ago I saw Carter Leffen's post (cool name) about reading a 1941 German Army Enigma message that had been listed as unsolved for decades. He isn't a cryptographer either, but Astra (GPT-6) doesn't mind: it worked the problem for about ten hours.[5]

That led me to Satoshi Tomokiyo's Cryptiana - the product of decades of one man's careful work documenting unsolved ciphers. His entry for it, listed as "Encoded Letter to Marshal Marmont (1807)", gives the clear first line and describes the system. It also notes that Marmont was using a code of only about 150 entries in 1811, so this one probably isn't large.[3][9]

Tomokiyo's site now points solvers to check against another guy, Daniel Bourdeau, who has read or partly read more than thirty ciphers from these lists in the last few weeks seemingly using foundation models as well. I read through his notes, saw he had attempted this one but stopped short, and wanted to see what I could do with it.[3][4]

“There is nothing to work on”

That has been the standing verdict on this cipher. The most recent solver notes on record put it flatly:

There is nothing to work on. The ciphertext is not published anywhere I can reach.[4]

Tomokiyo's page quotes only the first line (the line you read above), and the rest exists solely as the plate shown in Lieutenant-Colonel J. Vilcoq's 1969 article in the Revue historique des Armées.[3][1] Stop looking there and the trail goes cold.

It shouldn't. The journal is online, on Persée, the French academic archive. The plate sits after printed page 24. It's 1,202 by 1,836 pixels, roughly nineteen pixels per sign.[1][6] A partial table for this cipher, compiled by the French cryptology historian Daniel Tant and hosted by ARCSI, already documents 33 letter values. Every one of its word-sign cells is blank.[2] Those two files are where this work begins.

How it reads

The letter has 1,300 cipher units and 155 distinct signs.[6] It's a homophonic cipher: common letters get several interchangeable signs, so that counting frequencies gets you nowhere.[7]

Tant's 33 published values account for 435 of the 1,300 units. The other two-thirds had to be worked out from the letter itself.[2][6]

This took about six hours of model execution time with GPT-6 Astra, and everything below came out of one image. There was no transcription to start from, because none existed: Astra cut the 1,202 by 1,836 plate into rows, read the signs, decided which of 175 hand-drawn marks were the same sign written twice, and only then began breaking the cipher. Transcription and cryptanalysis are usually separate skills, often separate careers. Here they ran as one workflow, and the plate stayed in the loop: proposed values were checked back against every occurrence of a sign on the image.[6]

How the key was found

  1. Transcribe. The plate was cut into row crops and read line by line. Every visibly different mark got a provisional name, with potential pen variants kept separate. This work reconciled the sections into 1,320 units and 175 provisional labels.[6]
  2. Fix what is already known. Tant's 33 letter values were taken as given. The ten ordinary letters spelling “CONSEQUENT” in row 14 were kept as plain text. Between them, this covered about a third of the units before any new search began.[2][6]
  3. Search. A solver assigned letters to the remaining signs by simulated annealing, scoring each candidate plaintext against French letter statistics (3-, 4- and 5-grams) drawn from Hugo, Dumas and Marmont's own memoirs.[8][6]
  4. Find the word-signs. Signs that kept breaking otherwise good French were tested as whole words instead of letters. Twenty-nine of them turned out to be words: de, que, les, vous, général and the rest. Two more stand for a doubled S.[6]
  5. Check every sign against the plate. Wherever a sign's proposed value made the French smoother, that proposition was compared with every other occurrence of that sign. The value was kept only if this benefit was realized across all instances.[6]
  6. Try to break it. The solver was rerun from scratch with Marmont's memoirs and every Napoleonic text removed from its language model. It recovered the same reading, so the key does not depend on the model having seen the history it was decoding.[6]

What a solution looks like

The solution to a cipher like this is an answer key, and it is the same object the clerk in Eugène's office had on his desk in March 1809. French headquarters worked from a pair of sheets: a tableau chiffrant, plain text down the left with the signs to use beside it, and its inverse, the tableau déchiffrant, for the officer at the other end.[1][3] The clerk went through the Viceroy's draft one letter at a time, choosing among the signs on offer for each, so that no two E's in a row need look alike, and dropped in a null now and then for good measure.[6] Marmont's own headquarters used a code of only about 150 entries in 1811, with nine different figures for E, and the British staff officer George Scovell broke it within two days, helped by the plain words Marmont's clerks kept leaving mixed in with the cipher.[3][9] Whoever wrote this letter was more careful.

What follows is the tableau chiffrant rebuilt. Down the left, the plain text: the twenty-six letters, then the fifteen whole French words that got a sign of their own. Most of the signs are things a clerk could write quickly: two-digit numbers, ordinary letters, Greek letters, a handful of typographic symbols. About seventy are invented marks with no printed equivalent. The full key applied to all 1,300 units, in order, with no corrections, produces the French that the rest of this post is built on.[6]

The original ask

Let's also take a look at the order that prompted our letter to be written. On 16 March Napoleon told Eugène to send Marmont, in cipher, the position of every French and allied army. Unsurprisingly, the cipher letter lists the same seven forces the order does, in the same sequence, with the same figures:[10]

The titles are Napoleon's marshals: the Duke of Danzig is Lefebvre, the Prince of Ponte-Corvo is Bernadotte, the Duke of Auerstaedt is Davout, and the Duke of Rivoli is Masséna. Oudinot commanded the grenadier reserve. Poniatowski led the army of the Duchy of Warsaw, Napoleon's Polish client state.[21]

Napoleon kept at it. On 24 March he told Eugène to stop letting Frenchmen cross Austrian territory to reach Dalmatia, and to write to Marmont in cipher again to hurry his preparations. On 27 March he assumed Eugène was writing Marmont "by every courier, by land and by sea."[14]

The letter was written in the last days of March 1809, after Eugène's letter of the 20th and before Austria crossed the Inn on 10 April.[16][23]

How the forecast held up

The letter was a forecast. Here is how it aged, claim by claim, in a war most people have never heard of:

The enemy was exactly where the letter said. The letter places the Austrians at Laibach, Villach and Salzburg and says they threaten the Tyrol "by way of Lintz." On 10 April, Archduke Charles crossed the Inn into Bavaria without declaring war.[23] The same morning his younger brother, Archduke John, crossed into Italy with two corps that had marched from Villach and Laibach.[20][31] A division under Jellacic came down from Salzburg toward Munich.[32] And a corps under the Marquis de Chasteler moved out of Carinthia, occupied Lienz, and marched on Innsbruck as the Tyrol rose in revolt.[22][32] Essentially, someone in that office knew where the enemy was assembling two weeks before he moved.

Napoleon’s friends were not. The letter told Marmont Austria was "hastening toward her ruin." Six days into the war, John beat Eugène at Sacile and chased him back to Verona.[31] The letter credited Poniatowski with thirty thousand Poles. In reality, he had about 17,000, fought a drawn battle at Raszyn on 19 April, and handed Warsaw to the Austrians four days later.[33][21]

The Russians were a press release. "The Russians are marching against Austria" is the one line in the letter that was policy rather than fact. On 21 March Napoleon had ordered Eugène to "inculcate by every means, through newspaper articles or otherwise, the idea that the Russians are marching on Austria."[12] Three days later he wrote to his ambassador in St Petersburg: "You do not tell me where the Russian troops are. If Russia does not march, I shall have Austria on my hands alone."[13] He did. The Tsar had promised at Erfurt to march and had privately assured Vienna he would avoid every collision.[28][23] His army crossed into Galicia on 3 June, when the war was nearly decided.[33]

Then Napoleon lost a battle. Nobody in that office could have imagined it: on 21 and 22 May, crossing the Danube below Vienna, he was beaten at Aspern-Essling by the same Archduke Charles, his first defeat in a major battle in ten years.[39] Marshal Lannes, one of his closest friends, died of his wounds.[39] Emperor Francis wrote that his brother was "the first to interrupt the fifteen years of military fortune of the proud enemy."[39]

Marmont's push. The letter told him not to be intimidated by "a few troops or a gathering of rabble." In the last days of April the rabble attacked first: Grenzer, the Croatian border militia Austria kept on its Ottoman frontier, drove his men off the Zrmanja heights in a rainstorm.[29][30] Then the letter's conclusion held after all. In mid-May Marmont attacked again, beat the Austrians at Pribudić, captured their commander Stoichevich, fought through Gračac and Gospić, and on 3 June marched into Laibach, the first town on the letter's list of enemy positions.[29] He kept going. His Army of Dalmatia reached the Danube in time for the second day of Wagram on 6 July, the largest battle Europe had ever seen, some 300,000 men on a flat plain under a thousand guns.[40][34] Austria lost, and lost the war with it.[40]

The ending. Napoleon made Marmont a marshal, with a note saying "between ourselves, you have not done enough to justify entirely my choice."[17] At the peace of Schönbrunn in October, Austria gave up a sixth of its subjects and its whole Adriatic coast.[41] Napoleon bundled those lands into the Illyrian Provinces, made Marmont their governor, and gave him a capital: Laibach.[35] The most isolated man in the Empire ended the year ruling the town the letter had warned him about.

If you want the whole war in half an hour, Epic History TV's two animated episodes are the best short introduction I know: Aspern-Essling 1809 (19 minutes) and Wagram 1809: Napoleon's Revenge (14 minutes).

So What Happened to Marmont?

In March 1809, Marmont was a divisional general on the wrong side of the Adriatic, reading a cipher letter about armies he could not see telling him where the enemy was and told him to march when the order came. He did execute, and the march is why he is remembered at all.[17]

He spent two years in Laibach building roads and schools, introducing the Code Napoléon, and putting locals into office in their own languages, and it is the one stretch of his career that nobody argues about.[35] The baton, grudging note and all, followed him to Spain, where Wellington broke his army at Salamanca in July 1812 and a shellburst broke his arm.[36]

Then the ending everyone knows him for. In April 1814, with the Allies at the gates of Paris, Marmont came to a private arrangement with them and marched his corps into their lines. It was the act that convinced Napoleon he had to abdicate.[37][17] "I made him a marshal and a duke, and he vilely betrayed me," the Emperor said, and the French language agreed: for a generation raguser, from his title Duke of Ragusa, meant to betray.[17] He served the Bourbons, voted to shoot Marshal Ney, and in 1830 was the general who failed to hold Paris for Charles X, who asked him to his face, "Will you betray us, as you betrayed him?"[17]

Marmont went into exile with the king, tutored Napoleon's son in Vienna, and died in Venice in 1852, the last of the marshals.[37] He spent his final years writing nine volumes of memoirs to argue his case, and that is where this letter comes back in. Volume three prints Eugène's letters to him of 8, 14 and 20 March 1809, the three the cipher's first line acknowledges.[38][16]

New to the record

Napoleon's order of 16 March has been in print since 1865.[10] What nobody had was the other end of it: what actually got said to the general on the far side of the Adriatic.

The first thing it adds is a missing word. In the printed edition, Napoleon's sentence to Marmont breaks off. Marmont is to beat what is in front of him and not let himself be masked "par une poignée de . . . . . . . ." (by a handful of…), and then a row of dots. The edition was printed from a copy held by Eugène's descendants, and I can't tell whether the words were illegible in that copy or left out by the Second Empire editors, whose handling of Napoleon's text has been criticized since the day it was published.[10][15] Either way, the cipher letter carries the same sentence from the receiving end, and it has no gap: Marmont is not to be intimidated by "quelques troupes ou un rassemblement de canailles."[6] A few troops, or a gathering of rabble. The relay is a paraphrase, so this is not proof of Napoleon's exact word. It is the first direct evidence of what the dots were hiding.

The rest of the value is in the differences. Napoleon's order says nothing about Austrian positions. The cipher letter adds them, and they match where the Austrian corps really were.[31][32] It adds Marmont's own corps and the reserves to the count against Austria. It carries a skeptical read on the Landwehr, the compulsory militia Austria had created by imperial patent on 9 June 1808, from an office that would be fighting them within weeks.[27] And the whole thing is built to persuade: a list of armies meant to show a man whose corps Napoleon counted at 13,000, with no land route home, that the odds were overwhelming.[11]

It's a small document, but it shows how Napoleon's headquarters talked to an isolated commander on the eve of a war: accurate about the enemy, generous about its friends.

It also leaves behind a working key of 155 signs for a cipher that until now had 33 published values and no word-signs.[2] If another letter in this system ever surfaces, it won't start from zero.

The soft spots

This is one reading of one letter from one low-resolution plate. As shown above, some signs rest on thin evidence, almost all because they appear exactly once.[6] Five are open in a way that touches the wording: His Majesty could as easily be the Emperor; "the army of Friuli" could be "in Friuli"; des troupes could be les troupes; one sign I read as empty could be the word par; and canailles may be singular.[6]

None of the five would change what the letter says. Tomokiyo reviewed the solution, and Cryptiana now lists the letter as solved, with the date corrected to 1809.

A problem nobody could afford

None of the material here was missing. Tant's table was public, Napoleon's correspondence has been in print since the 1860s, and Marmont's memoirs are on Project Gutenberg.[2][10][16] A patient specialist could have done this in 1970. But it would have meant weeks of a specialist’s time: period French, a steady eye for 1,300 hand-drawn signs, and the statistics, all spent on one plate in one army journal. People with those skills exist, and they have more important problems to solve. So the letter sat unread, because no one who could read it could justify the time.

I spent six hours of model time and a few evenings of my own. Tomokiyo says he's receiving solutions faster than he can record them.[3] I’m sure few of these are from cryptographers. A year ago that sentence probably wouldn't have made sense.

I'd guess most "unsolved" lists, in most fields, hold more problems like this than anyone assumes. Those lists are about to get a lot shorter, and the people shortening them will increasingly be people who were simply curious.

The full solution package, with a script that regenerates the reading, is available for download. Two weeks before the war In February 1809, Vienna decided on war.[23] Napoleon had deposed the Spanish Bourbons the previous spring and taken their kingdom for his brother, and Vienna concluded that the Habsburgs were next unless it struck while his best troops were tied down in Spain.[24][23] On 8 February the Austrian Empire resolved to fight Napoleon, with the war party pointing at the French disaster at Bailén in Spain, where an entire French corps had surrendered the previous July.[26][25] Archduke Charles was the Austrian Emperor's younger brother and the best general the Habsburgs had.[19] He had spent three years rebuilding the army: 340,000 regulars, plus a new Landwehr militia on paper at 240,000.[26][27] Everyone could see what was coming. Napoleon had a specific problem, and its name was Marmont. Marmont, a personal friend of the Emperor, had been entrusted with what were called the "finest" troops in the theater (about 13,000 men by Napoleon's own count), and they were parked in Dalmatia on the far side of the Adriatic.[29][11] Austrian territory sat between them and every other French army. If war came, Marmont would be the most isolated general in the Empire. So on 16 March 1809, Napoleon wrote from Paris to his stepson Eugène, the Viceroy of Italy, and told him to send Marmont a letter.[18] It was to lay out where every French and allied army stood. It was to go "dans une lettre chiffrée et par un officier intelligent": in cipher, carried by an intelligent officer.[10] That letter, or one written to exactly that order, survives. Its first line is in plain French:[3] Vous avez dû recevoir, Monsieur le Général Marmont, mes lettres des 8, 14 et 20 courant.then 24 rows of cipher After that come twenty-four rows of two-digit numbers, stray letters, and invented symbols. Plate from J. Vilcoq, "Le Chiffre sous le Premier Empire," Revue historique des Armées 25(4), 1969, following p. 24. Digitized by Persée. The key didn't survive, and for 217 years nobody alive could read it. Why this one I've never broken a cipher. A week ago I saw Carter Leffen's post (cool name) about reading a 1941 German Army Enigma message that had been listed as unsolved for decades. He isn't a cryptographer either, but Astra (GPT-6) doesn't mind: it worked the problem for about ten hours.[5] That led me to Satoshi Tomokiyo's Cryptiana - the product of decades of one man's careful work documenting unsolved ciphers. His entry for it, listed as "Encoded Letter to Marshal Marmont (1807)", gives the clear first line and describes the system. It also notes that Marmont was using a code of only about 150 entries in 1811, so this one probably isn't large.[3][9] Tomokiyo's site now points solvers to check against another guy, Daniel Bourdeau, who has read or partly read more than thirty ciphers from these lists in the last few weeks seemingly using foundation models as well. I read through his notes, saw he had attempted this one but stopped short, and wanted to see what I could do with it.[3][4] “There is nothing to work on” That has been the standing verdict on this cipher. The most recent solver notes on record put it flatly: There is nothing to work on. The ciphertext is not published anywhere I can reach.[4] Tomokiyo's page quotes only the first line (the line you read above), and the rest exists solely as the plate shown in Lieutenant-Colonel J. Vilcoq's 1969 article in the Revue historique des Armées.[3][1] Stop looking there and the trail goes cold. It shouldn't. The journal is online, on Persée, the French academic archive. The plate sits after printed page 24. It's 1,202 by 1,836 pixels, roughly nineteen pixels per sign.[1][6] A partial table for this cipher, compiled by the French cryptology historian Daniel Tant and hosted by ARCSI, already documents 33 letter values. Every one of its word-sign cells is blank.[2] Those two files are where this work begins. How it reads The letter has 1,300 cipher units and 155 distinct signs.[6] It's a homophonic cipher: common letters get several interchangeable signs, so that counting frequencies gets you nowhere.[7] 1,300cipher units155distinct signs29signs for whole words33letter values published (Tant) Tant's 33 published values account for 435 of the 1,300 units. The other two-thirds had to be worked out from the letter itself.[2][6] 1,300cipher units 435readable from Tant's table · 33%865worked out from the letter · 67% This took about six hours of model execution time with GPT-6 Astra, and everything below came out of one image. There was no transcription to start from, because none existed: Astra cut the 1,202 by 1,836 plate into rows, read the signs, decided which of 175 hand-drawn marks were the same sign written twice, and only then began breaking the cipher. Transcription and cryptanalysis are usually separate skills, often separate careers. Here they ran as one workflow, and the plate stayed in the loop: proposed values were checked back against every occurrence of a sign on the image.[6] How the key was found Transcribe. The plate was cut into row crops and read line by line. Every visibly different mark got a provisional name, with potential pen variants kept separate. This work reconciled the sections into 1,320 units and 175 provisional labels.[6] Fix what is already known. Tant's 33 letter values were taken as given. The ten ordinary letters spelling “CONSEQUENT” in row 14 were kept as plain text. Between them, this covered about a third of the units before any new search began.[2][6] Search. A solver assigned letters to the remaining signs by simulated annealing, scoring each candidate plaintext against French letter statistics (3-, 4- and 5-grams) drawn from Hugo, Dumas and Marmont's own memoirs.[8][6] Find the word-signs. Signs that kept breaking otherwise good French were tested as whole words instead of letters. Twenty-nine of them turned out to be words: de, que, les, vous, général and the rest. Two more stand for a doubled S.[6] Check every sign against the plate. Wherever a sign's proposed value made the French smoother, that proposition was compared with every other occurrence of that sign. The value was kept only if this benefit was realized across all instances.[6] Try to break it. The solver was rerun from scratch with Marmont's memoirs and every Napoleonic text removed from its language model. It recovered the same reading, so the key does not depend on the model having seen the history it was decoding.[6] What a solution looks like The solution to a cipher like this is an answer key, and it is the same object the clerk in Eugène's office had on his desk in March 1809. French headquarters worked from a pair of sheets: a tableau chiffrant, plain text down the left with the signs to use beside it, and its inverse, the tableau déchiffrant, for the officer at the other end.[1][3] The clerk went through the Viceroy's draft one letter at a time, choosing among the signs on offer for each, so that no two E's in a row need look alike, and dropped in a null now and then for good measure.[6] Marmont's own headquarters used a code of only about 150 entries in 1811, with nine different figures for E, and the British staff officer George Scovell broke it within two days, helped by the plain words Marmont's clerks kept leaving mixed in with the cipher.[3][9] Whoever wrote this letter was more careful. What follows is the tableau chiffrant rebuilt. Down the left, the plain text: the twenty-six letters, then the fifteen whole French words that got a sign of their own. Most of the signs are things a clerk could write quickly: two-digit numbers, ordinary letters, Greek letters, a handful of typographic symbols. About seventy are invented marks with no printed equivalent. The full key applied to all 1,300 units, in order, with no corrections, produces the French that the rest of this post is built on.[6] Click a letter to see its signs. The letter Applied in order, with no corrections, the tableau chiffrant gives: to général marmontfrom the viceroy's headquartersdate late march 1809 [Those letters] contained the orders and instructions which [His Majesty] charged me to give you. I hasten today to acquaint you with the disposition of French and allied armies. The Duke of Danzig, at the head of forty thousand Bavarians, occupies Munich and Passau. Prince Poniatowski, at the head of thirty thousand Poles, is camped on the Vistula, threatening Cracow. The Prince of Ponte-Corvo commands the Saxon army, camped in front of Dresden, and the Duke of Auerstaedt occupies Bayreuth with eighty thousand French troops. The Duke of Rivoli commands sixty thousand men quartered at Ulm and Donauwörth. [General] Oudinot, with the elite corps comprising forty thousand men, is at Augsburg and along the Lech. The Russians are marching against Austria, and the army [of] Friuli today numbers eighty thousand men. Add the Dalmatian corps, without counting the reserves being organized everywhere in the rear, and you see that Austria will be attacked at once on every side. She is consequently hastening toward her ruin. When you receive the order to march, you must not allow yourself to be intimidated by a few troops or a gathering of rabble. I continue to await news from you with impatience. The Austrians are still at Laybach, Klagenfurth, Villach and Salzburg, and appear to threaten the Tyrol by way of Lintz. Yet one would think that they are considering sending troops into Galicia to oppose the Russians. These dispositions would suggest that their campaign plan has been upset before war has even been declared. There is, however, still nothing definite. The militia have been called into active service, and although efforts have been made to excite people, it has not yet been proved that these levies will provide much reinforcement for the army. 24 rows · 1,300 units · 155 signs Download the solution package (zip, 4 MB). On 16 March Napoleon told Eugène to send Marmont, in cipher, the position of every French and allied army. Unsurprisingly, the cipher letter lists the same seven forces the order does, in the same sequence, with the same figures:[10] ForceNapoleon to Eugène, 16 March 1809The cipher letter Duke of Danzig, Bavarians40,000, between Munich and Passauforty thousand, Munich and Passau Poniatowski, Poles30,000, Vistula, threatening Cracowthirty thousand, Vistula, threatening Cracow Ponte-Corvo, Saxonsbefore Dresdenin front of Dresden Duke of Auerstaedt80,000, Bayreutheighty thousand, Bayreuth Duke of Rivoli60,000, Ulm and Donauwörthsixty thousand, Ulm and Donauwörth Oudinot40,000, Augsburg and the Lechforty thousand, Augsburg and the Lech Russiansmarching on Austriamarching on Austria The titles are Napoleon's marshals: the Duke of Danzig is Lefebvre, the Prince of Ponte-Corvo is Bernadotte, the Duke of Auerstaedt is Davout, and the Duke of Rivoli is Masséna. Oudinot commanded the grenadier reserve. Poniatowski led the army of the Duchy of Warsaw, Napoleon's Polish client state.[21] ▲scroll the page▼Napoleon to Eugène, 16 March 1809 (no. 14908). Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, vol. 18, p. 358 (Paris, 1865), via archive.org. Napoleon kept at it. On 24 March he told Eugène to stop letting Frenchmen cross Austrian territory to reach Dalmatia, and to write to Marmont in cipher again to hurry his preparations. On 27 March he assumed Eugène was writing Marmont "by every courier, by land and by sea."[14] The letter was written in the last days of March 1809, after Eugène's letter of the 20th and before Austria crossed the Inn on 10 April.[16][23] How the forecast held up The letter was a forecast. Here is how it aged, claim by claim, in a war most people have never heard of: The enemy was exactly where the letter said. The letter places the Austrians at Laibach, Villach and Salzburg and says they threaten the Tyrol "by way of Lintz." On 10 April, Archduke Charles crossed the Inn into Bavaria without declaring war.[23] The same morning his younger brother, Archduke John, crossed into Italy with two corps that had marched from Villach and Laibach.[20][31] A division under Jellacic came down from Salzburg toward Munich.[32] And a corps under the Marquis de Chasteler moved out of Carinthia, occupied Lienz, and marched on Innsbruck as the Tyrol rose in revolt.[22][32] Essentially, someone in that office knew where the enemy was assembling two weeks before he moved. Napoleon’s friends were not. The letter told Marmont Austria was "hastening toward her ruin." Six days into the war, John beat Eugène at Sacile and chased him back to Verona.[31] The letter credited Poniatowski with thirty thousand Poles. In reality, he had about 17,000, fought a drawn battle at Raszyn on 19 April, and handed Warsaw to the Austrians four days later.[33][21] The Russians were a press release. "The Russians are marching against Austria" is the one line in the letter that was policy rather than fact. On 21 March Napoleon had ordered Eugène to "inculcate by every means, through newspaper articles or otherwise, the idea that the Russians are marching on Austria."[12] Three days later he wrote to his ambassador in St Petersburg: "You do not tell me where the Russian troops are. If Russia does not march, I shall have Austria on my hands alone."[13] He did. The Tsar had promised at Erfurt to march and had privately assured Vienna he would avoid every collision.[28][23] His army crossed into Galicia on 3 June, when the war was nearly decided.[33] Then Napoleon lost a battle. Nobody in that office could have imagined it: on 21 and 22 May, crossing the Danube below Vienna, he was beaten at Aspern-Essling by the same Archduke Charles, his first defeat in a major battle in ten years.[39] Marshal Lannes, one of his closest friends, died of his wounds.[39] Emperor Francis wrote that his brother was "the first to interrupt the fifteen years of military fortune of the proud enemy."[39] Marmont's push. The letter told him not to be intimidated by "a few troops or a gathering of rabble." In the last days of April the rabble attacked first: Grenzer, the Croatian border militia Austria kept on its Ottoman frontier, drove his men off the Zrmanja heights in a rainstorm.[29][30] Then the letter's conclusion held after all. In mid-May Marmont attacked again, beat the Austrians at Pribudić, captured their commander Stoichevich, fought through Gračac and Gospić, and on 3 June marched into Laibach, the first town on the letter's list of enemy positions.[29] He kept going. His Army of Dalmatia reached the Danube in time for the second day of Wagram on 6 July, the largest battle Europe had ever seen, some 300,000 men on a flat plain under a thousand guns.[40][34] Austria lost, and lost the war with it.[40] The ending. Napoleon made Marmont a marshal, with a note saying "between ourselves, you have not done enough to justify entirely my choice."[17] At the peace of Schönbrunn in October, Austria gave up a sixth of its subjects and its whole Adriatic coast.[41] Napoleon bundled those lands into the Illyrian Provinces, made Marmont their governor, and gave him a capital: Laibach.[35] The most isolated man in the Empire ended the year ruling the town the letter had warned him about. If you want the whole war in half an hour, Epic History TV's two animated episodes are the best short introduction I know: Aspern-Essling 1809 (19 minutes) and Wagram 1809: Napoleon's Revenge (14 minutes). So What Happened to Marmont? In March 1809, Marmont was a divisional general on the wrong side of the Adriatic, reading a cipher letter about armies he could not see telling him where the enemy was and told him to march when the order came. He did execute, and the march is why he is remembered at all.[17] He spent two years in Laibach building roads and schools, introducing the Code Napoléon, and putting locals into office in their own languages, and it is the one stretch of his career that nobody argues about.[35] The baton, grudging note and all, followed him to Spain, where Wellington broke his army at Salamanca in July 1812 and a shellburst broke his arm.[36] Then the ending everyone knows him for. In April 1814, with the Allies at the gates of Paris, Marmont came to a private arrangement with them and marched his corps into their lines. It was the act that convinced Napoleon he had to abdicate.[37][17] "I made him a marshal and a duke, and he vilely betrayed me," the Emperor said, and the French language agreed: for a generation raguser, from his title Duke of Ragusa, meant to betray.[17] He served the Bourbons, voted to shoot Marshal Ney, and in 1830 was the general who failed to hold Paris for Charles X, who asked him to his face, "Will you betray us, as you betrayed him?"[17] Marmont went into exile with the king, tutored Napoleon's son in Vienna, and died in Venice in 1852, the last of the marshals.[37] He spent his final years writing nine volumes of memoirs to argue his case, and that is where this letter comes back in. Volume three prints Eugène's letters to him of 8, 14 and 20 March 1809, the three the cipher's first line acknowledges.[38][16] New to the record Napoleon's order of 16 March has been in print since 1865.[10] What nobody had was the other end of it: what actually got said to the general on the far side of the Adriatic. The first thing it adds is a missing word. In the printed edition, Napoleon's sentence to Marmont breaks off. Marmont is to beat what is in front of him and not let himself be masked "par une poignée de . . . . . . . ." (by a handful of…), and then a row of dots. The edition was printed from a copy held by Eugène's descendants, and I can't tell whether the words were illegible in that copy or left out by the Second Empire editors, whose handling of Napoleon's text has been criticized since the day it was published.[10][15] Either way, the cipher letter carries the same sentence from the receiving end, and it has no gap: Marmont is not to be intimidated by "quelques troupes ou un rassemblement de canailles."[6] A few troops, or a gathering of rabble. The relay is a paraphrase, so this is not proof of Napoleon's exact word. It is the first direct evidence of what the dots were hiding. The rest of the value is in the differences. Napoleon's order says nothing about Austrian positions. The cipher letter adds them, and they match where the Austrian corps really were.[31][32] It adds Marmont's own corps and the reserves to the count against Austria. It carries a skeptical read on the Landwehr, the compulsory militia Austria had created by imperial patent on 9 June 1808, from an office that would be fighting them within weeks.[27] And the whole thing is built to persuade: a list of armies meant to show a man whose corps Napoleon counted at 13,000, with no land route home, that the odds were overwhelming.[11] It's a small document, but it shows how Napoleon's headquarters talked to an isolated commander on the eve of a war: accurate about the enemy, generous about its friends. It also leaves behind a working key of 155 signs for a cipher that until now had 33 published values and no word-signs.[2] If another letter in this system ever surfaces, it won't start from zero. The soft spots This is one reading of one letter from one low-resolution plate. As shown above, some signs rest on thin evidence, almost all because they appear exactly once.[6] Five are open in a way that touches the wording: His Majesty could as easily be the Emperor; "the army of Friuli" could be "in Friuli"; des troupes could be les troupes; one sign I read as empty could be the word par; and canailles may be singular.[6] None of the five would change what the letter says. Tomokiyo reviewed the solution, and Cryptiana now lists the letter as solved, with the date corrected to 1809. A problem nobody could afford None of the material here was missing. Tant's table was public, Napoleon's correspondence has been in print since the 1860s, and Marmont's memoirs are on Project Gutenberg.[2][10][16] A patient specialist could have done this in 1970. But it would have meant weeks of a specialist’s time: period French, a steady eye for 1,300 hand-drawn signs, and the statistics, all spent on one plate in one army journal. People with those skills exist, and they have more important problems to solve. So the letter sat unread, because no one who could read it could justify the time. I spent six hours of model time and a few evenings of my own. Tomokiyo says he's receiving solutions faster than he can record them.[3] I’m sure few of these are from cryptographers. A year ago that sentence probably wouldn't have made sense. I'd guess most "unsolved" lists, in most fields, hold more problems like this than anyone assumes. blocks.html_en: The solution to a cipher like this is an answer key, and it is the same object the clerk in Eugène's office had on his desk in March 1809. French headquarters worked from a pair of sheets: a tableau chiffrant, plain text down the left with the signs to use beside it, and its inverse, the tableau déchiffrant, for the officer at the other end.[1][3] The clerk went through the Viceroy's draft one letter at a time, choosing among the signs on offer for each, so that no two E's in a row need look alike, and dropped in a null now and then for good measure.[6] Marmont's own headquarters used a code of only about 150 entries in 1811, with nine different figures for E, and the British staff officer George Scovell broke it within two days, helped by the plain words Marmont's clerks kept leaving mixed in with the cipher.[3][9] Whoever wrote this letter was more careful.

blocks.html_en: The enemy was exactly where the letter said. The letter places the Austrians at Laibach, Villach and Salzburg and says they threaten the Tyrol "by way of Lintz." On 10 April, Archduke Charles crossed the Inn into Bavaria without declaring war.[23] The same morning his younger brother, Archduke John, crossed into Italy with two corps that had marched from Villach and Laibach.[20][31] A division under Jellacic came down from Salzburg toward Munich.[32] And a corps under the Marquis de Chasteler moved out of Carinthia, occupied Lienz, and marched on Innsbruck as the Tyrol rose in revolt.[22][32] Essentially, someone in that office knew where the enemy was assembling two weeks before he moved.

blocks.html_en: The Russians were a press release. "The Russians are marching against Austria" is the one line in the letter that was policy rather than fact. On 21 March Napoleon had ordered Eugène to "inculcate by every means, through newspaper articles or otherwise, the idea that the Russians are marching on Austria."[12] Three days later he wrote to his ambassador in St Petersburg: "You do not tell me where the Russian troops are. If Russia does not march, I shall have Austria on my hands alone."[13] He did. The Tsar had promised at Erfurt to march and had privately assured Vienna he would avoid every collision.[28][23] His army crossed into Galicia on 3 June, when the war was nearly decided.[33]

blocks.html_en: Marmont's push. The letter told him not to be intimidated by "a few troops or a gathering of rabble." In the last days of April the rabble attacked first: Grenzer, the Croatian border militia Austria kept on its Ottoman frontier, drove his men off the Zrmanja heights in a rainstorm.[29][30] Then the letter's conclusion held after all. In mid-May Marmont attacked again, beat the Austrians at Pribudić, captured their commander Stoichevich, fought through Gračac and Gospić, and on 3 June marched into Laibach, the first town on the letter's list of enemy positions.[29] He kept going. His Army of Dalmatia reached the Danube in time for the second day of Wagram on 6 July, the largest battle Europe had ever seen, some 300,000 men on a flat plain under a thousand guns.[40][34] Austria lost, and lost the war with it.[40]

blocks.html_en: The ending. Napoleon made Marmont a marshal, with a note saying "between ourselves, you have not done enough to justify entirely my choice."[17] At the peace of Schönbrunn in October, Austria gave up a sixth of its subjects and its whole Adriatic coast.[41] Napoleon bundled those lands into the Illyrian Provinces, made Marmont their governor, and gave him a capital: Laibach.[35] The most isolated man in the Empire ended the year ruling the town the letter had warned him about.

blocks.html_en: Then the ending everyone knows him for. In April 1814, with the Allies at the gates of Paris, Marmont came to a private arrangement with them and marched his corps into their lines. It was the act that convinced Napoleon he had to abdicate.[37][17] "I made him a marshal and a duke, and he vilely betrayed me," the Emperor said, and the French language agreed: for a generation raguser, from his title Duke of Ragusa, meant to betray.[17] He served the Bourbons, voted to shoot Marshal Ney, and in 1830 was the general who failed to hold Paris for Charles X, who asked him to his face, "Will you betray us, as you betrayed him?"[17]

blocks.html_en: The first thing it adds is a missing word. In the printed edition, Napoleon's sentence to Marmont breaks off. Marmont is to beat what is in front of him and not let himself be masked "par une poignée de . . . . . . . ." (by a handful of…), and then a row of dots. The edition was printed from a copy held by Eugène's descendants, and I can't tell whether the words were illegible in that copy or left out by the Second Empire editors, whose handling of Napoleon's text has been criticized since the day it was published.[10][15] Either way, the cipher letter carries the same sentence from the receiving end, and it has no gap: Marmont is not to be intimidated by "quelques troupes ou un rassemblement de canailles."[6] A few troops, or a gathering of rabble. The relay is a paraphrase, so this is not proof of Napoleon's exact word. It is the first direct evidence of what the dots were hiding.

blocks.html_en: The rest of the value is in the differences. Napoleon's order says nothing about Austrian positions. The cipher letter adds them, and they match where the Austrian corps really were.[31][32] It adds Marmont's own corps and the reserves to the count against Austria. It carries a skeptical read on the Landwehr, the compulsory militia Austria had created by imperial patent on 9 June 1808, from an office that would be fighting them within weeks.[27] And the whole thing is built to persuade: a list of armies meant to show a man whose corps Napoleon counted at 13,000, with no land route home, that the odds were overwhelming.[11]

Breaking the Marmont Cipher1809

A Napoleonic war briefing, unread for 217 years

abstract

A letter to General Marmont has sat on the standard list of unsolved historical ciphers, known only from a single reproduction in a 1969 French army journal that carries the wrong date.[1] This post gives a full working reading, produced end-to-end from that single scanned plate, redates the letter to March 1809, and places it in the two weeks before Austria invaded Bavaria. The full solution package, with a script that regenerates the reading, is available for download.

Two weeks before the war

In February 1809, Vienna decided on war.[23] Napoleon had deposed the Spanish Bourbons the previous spring and taken their kingdom for his brother, and Vienna concluded that the Habsburgs were next unless it struck while his best troops were tied down in Spain.[24][23] On 8 February the Austrian Empire resolved to fight Napoleon, with the war party pointing at the French disaster at Bailén in Spain, where an entire French corps had surrendered the previous July.[26][25] Archduke Charles was the Austrian Emperor's younger brother and the best general the Habsburgs had.[19] He had spent three years rebuilding the army: 340,000 regulars, plus a new Landwehr militia on paper at 240,000.[26][27] Everyone could see what was coming.

Napoleon had a specific problem, and its name was Marmont.

Marmont, a personal friend of the Emperor, had been entrusted with what were called the "finest" troops in the theater (about 13,000 men by Napoleon's own count), and they were parked in Dalmatia on the far side of the Adriatic.[29][11] Austrian territory sat between them and every other French army. If war came, Marmont would be the most isolated general in the Empire.

So on 16 March 1809, Napoleon wrote from Paris to his stepson Eugène, the Viceroy of Italy, and told him to send Marmont a letter.[18] It was to lay out where every French and allied army stood. It was to go "dans une lettre chiffrée et par un officier intelligent": in cipher, carried by an intelligent officer.[10]

That letter, or one written to exactly that order, survives. Its first line is in plain French:[3]

Vous avez dû recevoir, Monsieur le Général Marmont, mes lettres des 8, 14 et 20 courant.

then 24 rows of cipher

After that come twenty-four rows of two-digit numbers, stray letters, and invented symbols.

The key didn't survive, and for 217 years nobody alive could read it.

为什么是这个

I've never broken a cipher. A week ago I saw Carter Leffen's post (cool name) about reading a 1941 German Army Enigma message that had been listed as unsolved for decades. He isn't a cryptographer either, but Astra (GPT-6) doesn't mind: it worked the problem for about ten hours.[5]

That led me to Satoshi Tomokiyo's Cryptiana - the product of decades of one man's careful work documenting unsolved ciphers. His entry for it, listed as "Encoded Letter to Marshal Marmont (1807)", gives the clear first line and describes the system. It also notes that Marmont was using a code of only about 150 entries in 1811, so this one probably isn't large.[3][9]

Tomokiyo's site now points solvers to check against another guy, Daniel Bourdeau, who has read or partly read more than thirty ciphers from these lists in the last few weeks seemingly using foundation models as well. I read through his notes, saw he had attempted this one but stopped short, and wanted to see what I could do with it.[3][4]

“There is nothing to work on”

That has been the standing verdict on this cipher. The most recent solver notes on record put it flatly:

There is nothing to work on. The ciphertext is not published anywhere I can reach.[4]

Tomokiyo's page quotes only the first line (the line you read above), and the rest exists solely as the plate shown in Lieutenant-Colonel J. Vilcoq's 1969 article in the Revue historique des Armées.[3][1] Stop looking there and the trail goes cold.

It shouldn't. The journal is online, on Persée, the French academic archive. The plate sits after printed page 24. It's 1,202 by 1,836 pixels, roughly nineteen pixels per sign.[1][6] A partial table for this cipher, compiled by the French cryptology historian Daniel Tant and hosted by ARCSI, already documents 33 letter values. Every one of its word-sign cells is blank.[2] Those two files are where this work begins.

读起来如何

The letter has 1,300 cipher units and 155 distinct signs.[6] It's a homophonic cipher: common letters get several interchangeable signs, so that counting frequencies gets you nowhere.[7]

Tant's 33 published values account for 435 of the 1,300 units. The other two-thirds had to be worked out from the letter itself.[2][6]

This took about six hours of model execution time with GPT-6 Astra, and everything below came out of one image. There was no transcription to start from, because none existed: Astra cut the 1,202 by 1,836 plate into rows, read the signs, decided which of 175 hand-drawn marks were the same sign written twice, and only then began breaking the cipher. Transcription and cryptanalysis are usually separate skills, often separate careers. Here they ran as one workflow, and the plate stayed in the loop: proposed values were checked back against every occurrence of a sign on the image.[6]

How the key was found

  1. Transcribe. The plate was cut into row crops and read line by line. Every visibly different mark got a provisional name, with potential pen variants kept separate. This work reconciled the sections into 1,320 units and 175 provisional labels.[6]
  2. Fix what is already known. Tant's 33 letter values were taken as given. The ten ordinary letters spelling “CONSEQUENT” in row 14 were kept as plain text. Between them, this covered about a third of the units before any new search began.[2][6]
  3. 搜索。 A solver assigned letters to the remaining signs by simulated annealing, scoring each candidate plaintext against French letter statistics (3-, 4- and 5-grams) drawn from Hugo, Dumas and Marmont's own memoirs.[8][6]
  4. Find the word-signs. Signs that kept breaking otherwise good French were tested as whole words instead of letters. Twenty-nine of them turned out to be words: de, que, les, vous, général and the rest. Two more stand for a doubled S.[6]
  5. Check every sign against the plate. Wherever a sign's proposed value made the French smoother, that proposition was compared with every other occurrence of that sign. The value was kept only if this benefit was realized across all instances.[6]
  6. Try to break it. The solver was rerun from scratch with Marmont's memoirs and every Napoleonic text removed from its language model. It recovered the same reading, so the key does not depend on the model having seen the history it was decoding.[6]

What a solution looks like

The solution to a cipher like this is an answer key, and it is the same object the clerk in Eugène's office had on his desk in March 1809. French headquarters worked from a pair of sheets: a tableau chiffrant, plain text down the left with the signs to use beside it, and its inverse, the tableau déchiffrant, for the officer at the other end.[1][3] The clerk went through the Viceroy's draft one letter at a time, choosing among the signs on offer for each, so that no two E's in a row need look alike, and dropped in a null now and then for good measure.[6] Marmont's own headquarters used a code of only about 150 entries in 1811, with nine different figures for E, and the British staff officer George Scovell broke it within two days, helped by the plain words Marmont's clerks kept leaving mixed in with the cipher.[3][9] Whoever wrote this letter was more careful.

What follows is the tableau chiffrant rebuilt. Down the left, the plain text: the twenty-six letters, then the fifteen whole French words that got a sign of their own. Most of the signs are things a clerk could write quickly: two-digit numbers, ordinary letters, Greek letters, a handful of typographic symbols. About seventy are invented marks with no printed equivalent. The full key applied to all 1,300 units, in order, with no corrections, produces the French that the rest of this post is built on.[6]

The original ask

Let's also take a look at the order that prompted our letter to be written. On 16 March Napoleon told Eugène to send Marmont, in cipher, the position of every French and allied army. Unsurprisingly, the cipher letter lists the same seven forces the order does, in the same sequence, with the same figures:[10]

The titles are Napoleon's marshals: the Duke of Danzig is Lefebvre, the Prince of Ponte-Corvo is Bernadotte, the Duke of Auerstaedt is Davout, and the Duke of Rivoli is Masséna. Oudinot commanded the grenadier reserve. Poniatowski led the army of the Duchy of Warsaw, Napoleon's Polish client state.[21]

Napoleon kept at it. On 24 March he told Eugène to stop letting Frenchmen cross Austrian territory to reach Dalmatia, and to write to Marmont in cipher again to hurry his preparations. On 27 March he assumed Eugène was writing Marmont "by every courier, by land and by sea."[14]

The letter was written in the last days of March 1809, after Eugène's letter of the 20th and before Austria crossed the Inn on 10 April.[16][23]

How the forecast held up

The letter was a forecast. Here is how it aged, claim by claim, in a war most people have never heard of:

The enemy was exactly where the letter said. The letter places the Austrians at Laibach, Villach and Salzburg and says they threaten the Tyrol "by way of Lintz." On 10 April, Archduke Charles crossed the Inn into Bavaria without declaring war.[23] The same morning his younger brother, Archduke John, crossed into Italy with two corps that had marched from Villach and Laibach.[20][31] A division under Jellacic came down from Salzburg toward Munich.[32] And a corps under the Marquis de Chasteler moved out of Carinthia, occupied Lienz, and marched on Innsbruck as the Tyrol rose in revolt.[22][32] Essentially, someone in that office knew where the enemy was assembling two weeks before he moved.

Napoleon’s friends were not. The letter told Marmont Austria was "hastening toward her ruin." Six days into the war, John beat Eugène at Sacile and chased him back to Verona.[31] The letter credited Poniatowski with thirty thousand Poles. In reality, he had about 17,000, fought a drawn battle at Raszyn on 19 April, and handed Warsaw to the Austrians four days later.[33][21]

The Russians were a press release. "The Russians are marching against Austria" is the one line in the letter that was policy rather than fact. On 21 March Napoleon had ordered Eugène to "inculcate by every means, through newspaper articles or otherwise, the idea that the Russians are marching on Austria."[12] Three days later he wrote to his ambassador in St Petersburg: "You do not tell me where the Russian troops are. If Russia does not march, I shall have Austria on my hands alone."[13] He did. The Tsar had promised at Erfurt to march and had privately assured Vienna he would avoid every collision.[28][23] His army crossed into Galicia on 3 June, when the war was nearly decided.[33]

Then Napoleon lost a battle. Nobody in that office could have imagined it: on 21 and 22 May, crossing the Danube below Vienna, he was beaten at Aspern-Essling by the same Archduke Charles, his first defeat in a major battle in ten years.[39] Marshal Lannes, one of his closest friends, died of his wounds.[39] Emperor Francis wrote that his brother was "the first to interrupt the fifteen years of military fortune of the proud enemy."[39]

Marmont's push. The letter told him not to be intimidated by "a few troops or a gathering of rabble." In the last days of April the rabble attacked first: Grenzer, the Croatian border militia Austria kept on its Ottoman frontier, drove his men off the Zrmanja heights in a rainstorm.[29][30] Then the letter's conclusion held after all. In mid-May Marmont attacked again, beat the Austrians at Pribudić, captured their commander Stoichevich, fought through Gračac and Gospić, and on 3 June marched into Laibach, the first town on the letter's list of enemy positions.[29] He kept going. His Army of Dalmatia reached the Danube in time for the second day of Wagram on 6 July, the largest battle Europe had ever seen, some 300,000 men on a flat plain under a thousand guns.[40][34] Austria lost, and lost the war with it.[40]

The ending. Napoleon made Marmont a marshal, with a note saying "between ourselves, you have not done enough to justify entirely my choice."[17] At the peace of Schönbrunn in October, Austria gave up a sixth of its subjects and its whole Adriatic coast.[41] Napoleon bundled those lands into the Illyrian Provinces, made Marmont their governor, and gave him a capital: Laibach.[35] The most isolated man in the Empire ended the year ruling the town the letter had warned him about.

If you want the whole war in half an hour, Epic History TV's two animated episodes are the best short introduction I know: Aspern-Essling 1809 (19 minutes) and Wagram 1809: Napoleon's Revenge (14 minutes).

So What Happened to Marmont?

In March 1809, Marmont was a divisional general on the wrong side of the Adriatic, reading a cipher letter about armies he could not see telling him where the enemy was and told him to march when the order came. He did execute, and the march is why he is remembered at all.[17]

He spent two years in Laibach building roads and schools, introducing the Code Napoléon, and putting locals into office in their own languages, and it is the one stretch of his career that nobody argues about.[35] The baton, grudging note and all, followed him to Spain, where Wellington broke his army at Salamanca in July 1812 and a shellburst broke his arm.[36]

Then the ending everyone knows him for. In April 1814, with the Allies at the gates of Paris, Marmont came to a private arrangement with them and marched his corps into their lines. It was the act that convinced Napoleon he had to abdicate.[37][17] "I made him a marshal and a duke, and he vilely betrayed me," the Emperor said, and the French language agreed: for a generation raguser, from his title Duke of Ragusa, meant to betray.[17] He served the Bourbons, voted to shoot Marshal Ney, and in 1830 was the general who failed to hold Paris for Charles X, who asked him to his face, "Will you betray us, as you betrayed him?"[17]

Marmont went into exile with the king, tutored Napoleon's son in Vienna, and died in Venice in 1852, the last of the marshals.[37] He spent his final years writing nine volumes of memoirs to argue his case, and that is where this letter comes back in. Volume three prints Eugène's letters to him of 8, 14 and 20 March 1809, the three the cipher's first line acknowledges.[38][16]

New to the record

Napoleon's order of 16 March has been in print since 1865.[10] What nobody had was the other end of it: what actually got said to the general on the far side of the Adriatic.

The first thing it adds is a missing word. In the printed edition, Napoleon's sentence to Marmont breaks off. Marmont is to beat what is in front of him and not let himself be masked "par une poignée de . . . . . . . ." (by a handful of…), and then a row of dots. The edition was printed from a copy held by Eugène's descendants, and I can't tell whether the words were illegible in that copy or left out by the Second Empire editors, whose handling of Napoleon's text has been criticized since the day it was published.[10][15] Either way, the cipher letter carries the same sentence from the receiving end, and it has no gap: Marmont is not to be intimidated by "quelques troupes ou un rassemblement de canailles."[6] A few troops, or a gathering of rabble. The relay is a paraphrase, so this is not proof of Napoleon's exact word. It is the first direct evidence of what the dots were hiding.

The rest of the value is in the differences. Napoleon's order says nothing about Austrian positions. The cipher letter adds them, and they match where the Austrian corps really were.[31][32] It adds Marmont's own corps and the reserves to the count against Austria. It carries a skeptical read on the Landwehr, the compulsory militia Austria had created by imperial patent on 9 June 1808, from an office that would be fighting them within weeks.[27] And the whole thing is built to persuade: a list of armies meant to show a man whose corps Napoleon counted at 13,000, with no land route home, that the odds were overwhelming.[11]

It's a small document, but it shows how Napoleon's headquarters talked to an isolated commander on the eve of a war: accurate about the enemy, generous about its friends.

It also leaves behind a working key of 155 signs for a cipher that until now had 33 published values and no word-signs.[2] If another letter in this system ever surfaces, it won't start from zero.

The soft spots

This is one reading of one letter from one low-resolution plate. As shown above, some signs rest on thin evidence, almost all because they appear exactly once.[6] Five are open in a way that touches the wording: His Majesty could as easily be the Emperor; "the army of Friuli" could be "in Friuli"; des troupes could be les troupes; one sign I read as empty could be the word par; and canailles may be singular.[6]

None of the five would change what the letter says. Tomokiyo reviewed the solution, and Cryptiana now lists the letter as solved, with the date corrected to 1809.

A problem nobody could afford

None of the material here was missing. Tant's table was public, Napoleon's correspondence has been in print since the 1860s, and Marmont's memoirs are on Project Gutenberg.[2][10][16] A patient specialist could have done this in 1970. But it would have meant weeks of a specialist’s time: period French, a steady eye for 1,300 hand-drawn signs, and the statistics, all spent on one plate in one army journal. People with those skills exist, and they have more important problems to solve. So the letter sat unread, because no one who could read it could justify the time.

I spent six hours of model time and a few evenings of my own. Tomokiyo says he's receiving solutions faster than he can record them.[3] I’m sure few of these are from cryptographers. A year ago that sentence probably wouldn't have made sense.

I'd guess most "unsolved" lists, in most fields, hold more problems like this than anyone assumes. Those lists are about to get a lot shorter, and the people shortening them will increasingly be people who were simply curious.
